claims.text: The government is the authority that runs a country: it provides public goods such as street lighting that firms cannot sell profitably to individual buyers, it raises revenue through taxes on income and spending, and it transfers some of that revenue to households through payments such as the old-age pension.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: A government may intervene because markets on their own can leave wants unmet: public goods are not profitable to sell, some sellers grow so dominant that buyers lose choice, and some economic outcomes, such as very unequal incomes, may be judged unfair, so intervention ranges from providing goods itself to taxing, subsidising and regulating.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: A government faces limits on what it can do: it spends what taxes and borrowing raise, a poorer country raises less, taxes may discourage the activity being taxed, and running an industry requires skill and information the government may lack, so its economic role is likely to be wider in a richer country than in a poorer one.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Consumers and firms behave differently toward government revenue and spending than toward their own money: people prefer to keep income they earn themselves, they may grow less willing to work or invest where they expect taxes to rise, and a firm lobby may secure a rule that helps its members but leaves buyers worse off, so the government weighs each new tax or rule for these reactions.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.
